Sometimes, the most manifest gains are won after the most Herculean of battles. For France to
establish that “force is the crime” to establish that the use of force without consent causing
injury, rape, fear or annoyance is a criminal act, took years; extraordinary courage from one
woman, and an uprising where other women stood in solidarity with her. France has adopted a
law that defines rape as any non-consensual sexual act, a milestone for the women in the
country, but overall, a strike against sexual violence. The law was passed in response to urgent
calls from society to infuse consent into the law, and make sure that the law protects sexual
autonomy, particularly with reference to women. Last year, Gisèle Pelicot fought her toughest
battle when she took the stand in court, in a case accusing her husband of drugging and allowing
her to be raped by several men, some complete strangers. In December last year, the court
granted 51 convictions in the case, but it was more significant for establishing consent as a
pillar of law. It has been well established that survivors of sexual violence have an arduous
journey bringing their case to a court of law, and many women from disadvantaged social and
economic backgrounds, indeed do not have that privilege. There is a great deal of stigma, and
worse, judgement of the survivors in cases of rape, as recent public statements in India by
leaders blaming the women have painfully underlined again, and again. Even when a case of
rape enters the trial stage, the chances of securing a conviction are not encouraging. According
to the NCRB’s data, conviction rates for rape were between 27%-28% from 2018 to 2022. And
this, despite the fact that Section 129 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita recognises “criminal
force”.


To establish sexual autonomy as the cornerstone of the judicial process, while a first step, is
scarcely all. Preventing sexual violence will also involve shaping community views on gender
roles, dismantling rigid patriarchal codes with a measure of law, but also awareness
programmes that begin early, and orienting the police force to these principles, besides
funnelling resources into assisting survivors cope with the trauma. The road ahead is long and
arduous; for the journey of the survivors to be eased, governments should start with a complete
intolerance for sexual violence, and a commitment to stand by survivors, employing empathy
in the investigation and trial processes. To do any less, would be an injustice that would
interrupt the momentum of the women’s ‘Arab Spring’ Pelicot had set in motion.


SOURCE:https://www.thehindu.com/opinion/editorial/consent-is-all-on-sexual-violence-
support-for-survivors/article70226300.ece

My two-year-old can spot Ambedkar anywhere. On the walls, in the streets, in photographs,
on the television. He’ll also point out if he sees someone wearing “Ambedkar kannadi”. The
same with Gandhi. He’s a Sanjay Subrahmanyan fan, and requests songs any time he meets
Sanjay maama. If only my husband and I could curate who gets to raise our son, we’d fill his
life with people and things that aligned with our beliefs like these. After all, we have curated
our own adult lives this way. Minimising interactions with those we are unable to reconcile
with on the important things. What I have discovered, however, is that it indeed does take a
village to raise a child.


Much as I want to be the primary influencer of his life, he is a being of his own, has always
been. And because he speaks, and he speaks a lot at so young an age, and because he isn’t
anxious about the world, and is looking at it with wonder and love, awe and joy, he has
interactions with several people, many ideas, vastly varied approaches to life every single day.
And it is impossible for me to handpick his world to be only touched by those whose
impeccable taste I approve of. It is his interactions with strangers that bring me the most delight
and, of course, concern.

And so, I’m trying to take the pressure off my son now, and apply it on to my own self — only
this time, to make myself softer. To set the example, by holding myself accountable to others,
I share my space with. By trying to figure out how to not fly into rage, and deal with conflict
with presence and control. To show him how much I love the softer things for him as well.
Embracing the Montessori way has helped somewhat at this stage, for it emphasises
independence and shows us that the precious reward of learning is indeed self-sufficiency. I
am far from the perfect human, and one who’s painfully aware of her own shortcomings. And
I don’t expect to raise a mythical, perfect human son either. But if I were to apply one of the
many writing lessons to my life, in raising my son it is: Show, don’t tell.


After all, monkey see, monkey do.

The recent tragedy involving three minor sisters who stepped off a ninth-floor balcony together
in an act of collective despair has forced a harrowing reckoning with a new, endemic form of
addiction. These children had lived almost entirely within a gaming world for months –
reportedly insulated from reality and withdrawn from school. When their access was abruptly
severed to break the cycle, the resulting “void” proved too much to bear. For them, the scolding
was not merely a lecture; it was a perceived threat to the only domain in which he felt a sense
of achievement and agency. These cases underscore a terrifying reality: when the “digital
tether” is snapped by force, the resulting panic is not a tantrum – it is a clinical withdrawal.


With over 568 million active gamers, the world’s largest user base, India sees addiction rates
between 3.5 and 7.2 per cent among its youth. To address this, we must move past the label of
“bad behaviour” and understand the mechanics of capture. Expert analysis has highlighted how
children are caught in “Ludic Loops” – repetitive cycles of challenge and rewards meticulously

designed by software engineers to be inescapable. When a child enters this state, they become
what experts call a “Digital Ghost.” They remain physically present at the dinner table but are
emotionally and psychologically absent. Their brain’s reward system has been rewired; the
nuanced pace of the physical world cannot compete with the high-speed chemical rush of the
screen. In this state, the child is responding to a deep chemical dependence where “unplugging”
feels like physical suffocation.


However, this biological capture does not occur in a vacuum; it is facilitated by a disappearing
physical reality. As we emerge as a global digital powerhouse, the question before us is whether
our physical “Third Spaces” for youth are vanishing under the weight of urban congestion and
high costs. Instead of reactive bans, we must advocate for “Safety by Design” rather than
punishment. The rising number of tragedies suggests that a shift in perspective is no longer
optional. We must realise the need for parental vigilance in the responsibility of building a
physical world worth inhabiting. This is a complex challenge involving biological,
psychological, and systemic factors. It is time to transform digital despair into real-world
connection by replacing force with empathy and systemic reform.

What caused this degradation across your favourite platforms and apps? One theory that has
gained traction is enshittification: the feeling that many of your digital experiences,
transactions, and services are not improving over time but are actually becoming worse due to
their makers’ updates. Enshittification, according to Doctorow, is a way of naming the process
through which internet platforms are being made deliberately worse for customers, by their
decision-makers, until they decay completely. “Here is how platforms die: first, they are good
to their users; then they abuse their users to make things better for their business customers;
finally, they abuse those business customers to claw back all the value for themselves. Then,
they die,” wrote Doctorow in a blog post in 2023. In other words: when your experience with
a shopping app or a streaming platform grows worse, much of this enshittification can be traced
back to the dominance of just a few Big Tech players, looser antitrust enforcement by
authorities, customers’ diminished capacity to control their digital experiences, and/or the
inability of tech workers to say no to exploitative bosses, according to the author.

Enshittification is also used to refer to a range of symptoms that degrade your experience as an
internet user or customer. Some examples include the insertion of advertisements, self-
preferencing by tech companies, unfair bias in search results, once-free features becoming paid,
genuine products being replaced with lower-value dupes, and more. Doctorow also points out
that apps offer massive potential for enshittification because app users often have less freedom
to block ads than users accessing the same platform via the web.

What’s in a military operation name? Quite a bit, actually. Despite being coordinated between
America’s Pentagon and Israel’s Kirya, Washington and Tel Aviv have decided to use two
separate op names for their Iran campaign – Op Epic Fury and Op Roaring Lion respectively.
Why two names? It’s all about political messaging. Having rechristened US’s department of
defence as department of war, Washington clearly wants to signal overwhelming power –
something that feeds into the narrative of US being No.1. Israel, meanwhile, is tapping into the
Judeo-Persian motif of the lion, signalling solidarity with old Persia against the Islamic
Republic.


All of these may seem like little mind games. But in the age of informationised warfare,
messaging is as important as cutting-edge drones. So, Op Midnight Hammer signalled a literal
battering of Iran’s nuclear infrastructure by US forces last year. But this exercise isn’t exactly
new. It all started with WWI and gained prominence in WWII, when Germany under Hitler
drew on historical and mythological figures to message German superiority. Hence, Op
Barbarossa – after Holy Roman Emperor Frederick I – for the German invasion of Soviet
Union.


US military began with colour-coded names such as Op Indigo – plan to prevent Nazis from
seizing Iceland – but later switched to a computerised naming system after Vietnam.
However, big ops get two-word names that are cleared by the Secretary of Defence, like Op
Enduring Freedom for Afghanistan and Op Odyssey Dawn for Libya. One exception: UK’s
op to retake the Falklands in 1982 was dubbed a very blah Op Corporate – said to be the next
available name on a Whitehall list. Closer home, we had India’s Op Cactus to thwart the
attempted coup in Maldives in 1988. If Op Parakram after the 2001 Parliament attack served
as a warning for Pakistan, Op Sindoor last year ensured justice for those widowed by the
Pahalgam terror attack. So, expect war names to get more creative, and political.

The recent electoral shift in Bharatiya Janata Party’s favour in West Bengal marks a significant
transformation in the state’s political landscape, traditionally dominated by regional forces like
the All India Trinamool Congress. Analysts attribute this outcome not merely to campaign
strategy but to a layered anti-incumbency sentiment that had been building over multiple
election cycles. Governance fatigue, allegations of corruption in welfare schemes, and internal
factionalism weakened the ruling establishment.

The BJP’s campaign leveraged central leadership visibility, grassroots mobilization, and a
narrative centered around governance efficiency and national integration. The party’s ability
to consolidate fragmented opposition votes, particularly in semi-urban belts, proved decisive.
Additionally, shifts in voter behaviour among youth and first-time voters reflected changing
aspirations tied to employment and development.

However, the election also highlights broader themes in Indian democracy—how long-
standing regional parties face structural challenges when confronted with national parties
possessing stronger organizational machinery and financial resources. The role of federal
dynamics, electoral financing, and digital campaigning has become increasingly pronounced.

While the TMC’s decline appears sharp, political observers caution against premature
conclusions about its complete marginalization, noting that regional identity politics and
grassroots networks can facilitate resurgence. Nonetheless, the verdict signals a recalibration
of political equations in eastern India and underscores the evolving nature of electoral mandates

The fragile ceasefire between Iran and the United States has come under severe strain following
renewed hostilities in early May 2026. On May 4, Iran launched a series of missile and drone
strikes targeting infrastructure in the United Arab Emirates, including a major oil facility at
Fujairah. The attacks mark the first direct strike on a Gulf state since the ceasefire was declared
in April, raising concerns about a full-scale resumption of conflict.

The escalation is closely linked to tensions in the Strait of Hormuz, a critical global chokepoint
through which nearly one-fifth of the world’s oil supply passes. Iran has effectively restricted
maritime movement in the region, while the United States has initiated military operations to
escort commercial vessels and restore navigation.

Global reactions have been swift, with multiple countries condemning the strikes and urging
de-escalation. The conflict has also triggered a sharp rise in global oil prices, reflecting fears
of supply disruptions and broader economic instability.

Analysts suggest that the renewed confrontation reflects deeper structural tensions, including
disputes over maritime security, regional influence, and stalled nuclear negotiations. While
diplomatic efforts continue, the situation underscores the volatility of the Gulf region and its
critical importance to global energy and geopolitical stability.

The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (TPA), serves as the foundational statute governing the
transfer of property between living persons in India, meticulously outlining the specific modes
through which such transfers can be lawfully effected. These modes, or specific transfers, each
possess distinct legal characteristics, rights, and obligations that are critical for the validity and
enforceability of the transaction. The first and most comprehensive mode is a Sale, defined
under Section 54 as the transfer of ownership in exchange for a price. It is a complete transfer
of all rights and interests from the seller to the buyer, fundamentally requiring a consideration
termed the price. A pivotal concept in a valid sale is that of a "marketable title," which refers

12 Minutes to CLAT                                               CLAT 2027 Mock Test - 20


to the seller’s ability to prove their ownership is free from reasonable doubt or litigation,
thereby ensuring the buyer receives a secure and undisputed interest in the property.


Another crucial mode is a Mortgage, involving the transfer of an interest in specific immovable
property for the purpose of securing a loan or the performance of an engagement. This area is
notably complex, encompassing various types such as a simple mortgage, where the property
is not delivered but the mortgagor binds themselves personally to repay; an English mortgage,
where the property is transferred absolutely to the creditor with a condition for re-transfer upon
repayment; and an equitable mortgage, created by depositing title deeds with the creditor. The
TPA meticulously delineates the rights and liabilities of both the mortgagor (the borrower) and
the mortgagee (the lender), including the mortgagor’s right of redemption and the mortgagee’s
power of sale. A Lease is a transfer of a right to enjoy a property for a specified period, in
consideration of a premium or rent paid periodically, and it creates a landlord-tenant

gratuitous transfer of existing movable or immovable property without any consideration, made
by a donor and accepted by the donee. The Act also recognizes an Exchange, where parties
transfer the ownership of one thing for the ownership of another, and the transfer of Actionable
Claims, which includes the transfer of rights to debts or beneficial interests in movable property
not in possession. Collectively, these defined modes provide a comprehensive legal framework
ensuring clarity, security, and fairness in all property transactions.

The architecture of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, rests upon a foundation of presumptions
and the principles of relevancy, meticulously detailed in its opening sections. Section 4 of the
Act introduces the crucial concept of presumptions, which are rules of law that dictate how a
court must or may approach certain facts. It delineates three distinct degrees. The first is when
the court "may presume" a fact, meaning the court enjoys a discretionary power to either regard
the fact as proved unless and until it is disproved, or to call for formal proof of it. The second


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                        24

12 Minutes to CLAT                                                CLAT 2027 Mock Test - 20


and stronger degree is when the court "shall presume". Here, the court is left with no discretion;
it is obliged to regard the fact as proved unless and until it is disproved. This creates a
mandatory presumption that shifts the evidentiary burden onto the opposing party. The third
and most absolute category is "conclusive proof". When a fact is declared to be conclusive
proof of another, the court is not permitted to entertain any evidence to the contrary. This
creates an irrebuttable presumption, where the existence of one fact is deemed to be the final
and incontrovertible truth of another.


Flowing from this framework of presumptions, the Act then establishes which facts are relevant
enough to be admitted for judicial scrutiny. Section 6 codifies the principle of res gestae,
rendering facts relevant that, though not strictly the fact in issue, are so connected with it as to
form part of the same transaction. This often applies to spontaneous declarations or
accompanying acts that lend veracity to the main event, such as the immediate outcry of a
victim. Expanding on this, Section 7 declares as relevant any facts which are the occasion,
cause, or effect of a fact in issue. For instance, the state of a lock after a burglary is relevant as
an effect of the crime. Furthermore, Section 8 establishes the enduring relevance of motive,
preparation, and conduct. While a strong motive may point towards guilt, and preparation
demonstrates a plan, the conduct of a person immediately after an alleged event—such as
fleeing the scene or attempting to dispose of evidence—is highly significant. Finally, Section
9 addresses facts which are necessary to explain or introduce a fact in issue. This provision is
the legal basis for test identification parades, where the fact that a witness identified an accused
shortly after the crime helps to corroborate their testimony in court. Collectively, these sections
form the gateway through which facts must pass to be considered admissible, ensuring that
judicial proceedings are grounded in logically probative material.

The Specific Relief Act, 1963, provides equitable remedies to enforce civil rights where
monetary compensation is inadequate. Part III of the Act deals with the Rectification of
Instruments, while Part IV governs the Rescission of Contracts. These provisions address two
distinct scenarios: correcting a written document to reflect the true agreement, or completely
canceling a contract when its formation was fundamentally flawed.


Section 26 of the Act empowers courts to rectify a written instrument that does not express the
real intention of the parties due to fraud or mutual mistake. The core principle is that a deed or
agreement should accurately mirror the actual contract between the parties. To obtain
rectification, the plaintiff must prove that a prior concluded contract existed and that, due to a
common error or fraudulent conduct, the formal document deviated from that agreement. The


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                        27

12 Minutes to CLAT                                                CLAT 2027 Mock Test - 20


court does not create a new contract but aligns the writing with the parties' genuine intent. Once
rectified, the instrument operates as if originally executed in its corrected form.


In contrast, Part IV (Sections 27 to 30) addresses the rescission of contracts, allowing a party
to have a voidable contract set aside. Rescission is typically available where consent was
obtained through coercion, undue influence, fraud, or misrepresentation. The party seeking
rescission must act promptly and generally restore any benefits received under the contract.
However, Section 27 provides specific defences against rescission. The court may refuse to
cancel a contract if the applicant has ratified it, expressly or impliedly; if, due to lapse of time
or third-party rights, the parties cannot be restored to their original positions; or if the contract
concerns a non-severable part of a property where the buyer has taken possession. These
defences ensure that rescission is not granted when it would be unjust or impractical.


Together, these provisions reflect the Act's commitment to substantive justice: rectification
polishes the instrument to reveal the true agreement, while rescission cancels the transaction
entirely when the foundation of consent is unsound, subject to protections for innocent parties
and practical limits on restitution.

The pharmaceutical industry routinely defends its practice of making incremental
modifications to existing drugs, adjusting dosage forms, delivery mechanisms, or combining
active ingredients and then filing fresh patent applications on these reformulated products. This
strategy, known as "evergreening," effectively extends a drug's period of market exclusivity
well beyond the original twenty-year patent term. Defenders of the practice argue that it
rewards genuine innovation and incentivises companies to invest in improvements that benefit
patients.Critics, however, contend that evergreening is fundamentally a legal manoeuvre rather
than a scientific one. Most reformulations offer no meaningful therapeutic advantage over the
original compound. The new patent does not reflect a discovery that advances medicine; it
reflects a corporation's determination to delay the entry of cheaper generic competitors. In
markets where healthcare budgets are constrained, this delay carries a real cost: governments
and patients continue to pay premium prices for a drug whose core molecule has long since
ceased to be proprietary.India's response to this problem has drawn international attention.
Section 3(d) of India's Patents Act requires that, to be patentable, a new form of a known
substance must demonstrate significantly enhanced therapeutic efficacy not merely a change
in form. Under this provision, the Supreme Court of India famously denied a patent extension
to a modified version of the cancer drug imatinib mesylate, ruling that the reformulation did
not cross the therapeutic efficacy threshold.The pharmaceutical industry challenged the Indian
provision vigorously, arguing that it sets an unusually high bar that will deter research
investment. But public health advocates responded that the standard is not punitive; it simply
ensures that patents reflect genuine medical advances rather than administrative creativity. The
core question in the evergreening debate is not whether pharmaceutical companies deserve to
profit from innovation; it is whether the law should reward paper innovation as though it were
the real thing.[Extracted with revisions and edits from discussions of pharmaceutical patent
